entry.title: A guild buff that could not leave its core
entry.summary: Metin2 mainline guild skills ran in the caster's body over one war map, and the game had no empire skills at all. How they were removed in 2019, came back in 2026, and became casts that run on every core with nobody performing them.
entry.content:
A guild is not on one core. Its members are logged in on every core of the mesh, and each core knows only its own players. In the Metin2 mainline engine a guild skill was computed by the caster's body, so the skill reached the guild's war members standing on the caster's war map and nobody else. A guild member on another core, or in another channel, was simply not part of it. For a guild-wide skill, that is the whole bug.

This post is about how long that limit lived in our code base, why the skills left in 2019, and what the second attempt in 2026 did differently. It ends with a gap I have not closed.

Guild skills in the Metin2 mainline engine​

The Metin2 mainline engine had guild skills only, in a fixed range of vnums from 151 up, and no empire skills of any kind. Each one was hardcoded by vnum. Using one was refused outside a guild war:

if (!UnderAnyWar() || !ch->GetWarMap())
{
    ch->ChatPacket(CHAT_TYPE_INFO, LC_TEXT("<길드> 길드 스킬은 길드전 중에만 사용할 수 있습니다."));
    return;
}

Inside a war, the skill called the war map. The war map walked its own set of characters and ran the caster's ComputeSkill on each war member of one guild. Two skills, 156 and 157, ran it a second time against the opposing guild; the rest only on the caster's own:

void CWarMap::ComputeSkill(LPCHARACTER pkCaster, uint32_t dwVnum, uint32_t dwLevel, uint32_t dwGuildID)
{
    FWarComputeSkill f(pkCaster, dwVnum, dwLevel, dwGuildID);
    std::for_each(m_set_pkChr.begin(), m_set_pkChr.end(), f);
}

That is the entire reach: one war map, hosted by one core, with the caster's body applying the skill to everyone on it. The level lived in a byte array on the guild, the cost came from a guild power pool, and the only moment you could use any of it was a war.

By the time our repository began in 2016 the war skills had become a loop over the guild's online members on the core, filtered by those standing on a war map, and a second family of guild skills had been added on top. It reached up to vnum 169, needed a guild level, paid from a second pool, was not war only, and applied to every online member on every core through a packet between cores. So the push to every core is older than our work. But each member computed the skill on himself, it was hardcoded per vnum, and it only did buffs on the guild's own members. Nothing in it could hit an enemy, and nothing in it could belong to an empire.

Removed in April 2019​

In February 2019 we wrote the first version of the composable skill system, where a skill became a tree of nodes. Guild skills did not fit it: they were war-only code keyed by vnum, and the nodes had no place for either.

So in April 2019 we removed them. About 1,200 lines went, among them the guild's use and cross-core handlers and the guild skill handlers of the client's guild window. We decided to keep guild skills out of gameplay and plan them for a later update. In August 2019 the old guild wars went as well, leaving only the skeleton. Some remains stayed in the engine: in 2023 the skill power for the whole guild range was set to return 0, and it still does.

Back in March 2026, shaped like the Metin2 mainline engine​

In March 2026 guild skills came back. A guild kept a table of levels and cooldowns, a packet between cores carried the changes, and a gskill command and a guild skill page in the client arrived. Costs and cooldowns moved to the guild. Skill data had left the database table, where it had been edited with no versioning, for the YAML files, so a guild skill was now a file like any other.

It was shaped like the Metin2 mainline engine. A guild skill went through the ordinary character path, and the code of that time said what was wrong with it in its own comment: the caster owns the skill instance, but the cooldown and the costs are owned by the guild. Every place that read a level, a cooldown or a cost had a branch on the guild skill type. The cast still ran in the caster's body, on the caster's core.

That was the second pass at the same limit, and it worked about as well as the first. A buff for every member of a guild still could not be computed anywhere, because no core holds every member.

Owners, and a cast with nobody performing it​

In August 2026, five months after the revival, we rebuilt it. One large change on 9 August split two things that had always been the same character: the owner of a cast and the performer of it.

The owner holds the skill: its level, its cooldown, its purse, the right to cast it, and who counts as ally and enemy. The performer is the character who pressed the button, and supplies the geometry, the weapon and the credit for a kill. For an ordinary skill both are one character and nothing changes. A guild skill is owned by the guild. An empire, which has no object of its own, became an owner too, with its state kept in server flags.

The second key is the one the title is about. A skill declares intracore: true, and the cast splits in two. The core where the button was pressed authorizes it: authority, cost, cooldown, all the checks. Then every core executes it, the pressing core included, through the same entry point, with no performer at all. This is the call site:

// An intracore cast splits in two: AUTHORISE here, where the button was
// pressed (authority, cost, cooldown -- all done above), then EXECUTE on
// every core including this one, through the same entry point, with no
// performer. This core is not privileged: a cast that could read whoever
// pressed would give his core different numbers from every sibling.
if (pkSk->bIntracore)
{
    SIM_TRACE_PICK("intracore");
    pkSkillInstance->UseSkill();

    const uint32_t unLevel = pkSkillInstance->GetUseLevel();
    const uint32_t dwSubjectId = pkSkillInstance->GetSubject()
        ? pkSkillInstance->GetSubject()->Id() : 0;

    CSkillManager::instance().BroadcastIntracore(pkSk->bSubjectKind, dwSubjectId,
        pkSk->unVnum, unLevel);
    CSkillManager::instance().ExecuteIntracore(pkSk->bSubjectKind, dwSubjectId,
        pkSk->unVnum, unLevel);

    m_dwLastSkillTime = get_dword_time();
    return true;
}

The packet carries the owner kind and id, the skill, and the level. Nothing else crosses. Each core rebuilds the owner from the id and asks it who is on each side on this core. A guild lists its members who are online here, or the online members of the guild it is at war with. An empire lists its players here. The union over all cores is the whole guild or the whole empire, and nobody is hit twice, because a player is online on exactly one core.

Two details were learned the hard way, by reading what would happen if we got them wrong. The level travels in the packet, so a core whose copy of the guild row is a moment behind still applies the number the caster paid for. And only the authorizing core stamps the cooldown. For a guild that is a write to the guild row, for an empire a server flag, and both fan out to the database core and the whole mesh. If every receiver stamped it, one cast would multiply that fan-out by the number of cores.

Nothing declares a skill safe to replicate. A cast can be computed identically on a sibling core exactly when the owner's state is present there and its formulas read nothing else, so the skill loader checks it when it reads the file. A skill that mentions the caster anywhere does not load, and the game core says which node and which field.

There is a price, and it shows in damage. With no attacker, a hit applies only the victim's half: the victim's own defense stands, without penetration, and nothing is read off an attacker's sheet. A kill has no owner, so it gives no experience and no drops. The shipped intracore damage skills accept players only.

Six skills the same night, and a pair​

The limit we closed is that a cast never left its core. The first clients of the change were six guild and empire skills, written the same night as the owner model, from 152 to 157. Skill 158 joined later that day, an empire skill called Giudizio dell'Impero: a mark on every enemy player of the empire, wherever they are logged in, five seconds of warning, then a ray at the place where each mark was planted. Dying, warping or logging out between the mark and the ray does not cancel it. Running away does.

On 21 October 2026 came the skill that answers it, 150, Santuario Stellare. It is a sanctuary of 12 meters that heals, shields and cleanses every player of the empire inside it for 20 seconds, and it carries a trait that zeroes the hits of 158. It is deliberately not intracore. An intracore cast has no performer and so no center, and this skill is nothing but a center, so it lives on the one core where it was planted. The pair is the clearest way I know to show the two reaches: 158 is every core, 150 is one place on one core.

The map-wide ones are different again. 155, 156 and 157 are empire skills where one node sweeps every entity on the map, which is still one core. They are not intracore, because a fight happens on one map and a timed run reads the performer on every tick, so they keep the caster. 156 puts one affect on every enemy on the map and hangs the damage under it, so the damage keeps the critical roll, the attacker's bonuses and a real killer. 155 has a trap in its own header: a child sweep under a map-wide parent still starts from the performer's sector tree, so an ally on the far side of the map finds nobody.

The war-only list still catches four of them​

The rule that guild skills work only in a guild war survived all of this. It is now a use policy with a list of vnums, and the list still holds 151 to 157. For 151 to 153, the guild skills, that is the Metin2 mainline rule doing what it always did. For the empire skills 154 to 157 it is a bug. An empire has no war, so those four are refused outside a guild war with the message that the skill can be used only in war. 150 and 158 are not on the list, which is why the pair above works.

The list is a policy, not part of the owner model, so the owner code never sees it. I filed it as an issue and have not touched the list yet.

Other things are still in the engine too. The GUILD_SKILL_* constants, 151 to 159, are still defined and exported to the client scripts. A new kind of owner is C++ work in three places and has no Lua door. And the headless simulator cannot show everything: one process is one core, and guild gold never decreases there because the database answer never comes.

entry.title: 25 skills disagreed with themselves
entry.summary: Every skill in the Metin2 mainline engine lives in three hand-kept copies, a server row and two client files, and they do not agree. How we found it by deleting copies, what the drift looked like, and what one file costs and buys.
entry.content:
In the Metin2 mainline engine a skill is written down three times: a row in the server database, a line in a client table, and a line in the client tooltip file. Nobody checks that the three say the same thing. When we finally deleted two of the copies in July 2026, we found 25 skills that told the client they could target a buffable NPC and told the server nothing, and 281 tooltip formulas copied from the skill configs, 17 of which had drifted from the engine's.

This post is about those three copies, how long we kept them by hand, and what it took to get down to one.

Three copies, already disagreeing​

The server side is the table skill_proto, read by the database core at boot. The client side is two text files: a skill table with the formulas, and a tooltip file that carries its own copy of the tooltip formula. The inherited data is the only evidence I can show for the Metin2 mainline engine, and only between the two client files, because the server rows are not in the tree.

Take the first four warrior skills. Skill 3 agrees with its tooltip. The other three do not:

skillclient tabletooltip file
1, three-way cut-(1.1*atk+(0.5*atk+1.5*str)*k)(1.1*MinATK + (0.1*MinATK + 1.5*STR)*SkillPoint) * 3
2, sword whirlwind-(3*atk+(0.8*atk+str*5+dex*3+con)*k)3*MinATK + (0.8*MinATK + STR*6 + DEX*2 + CON) * SkillPoint
4, sword aura(100+str+lv*3)*k(100 + STR) * SkillPoint

Skill 1 uses 0.5 of the attack in one file and 0.1 in the other (the * 3 is the three hits, not a disagreement). Skill 2 swaps strength 5 and dexterity 3 for 6 and 2. The tooltip for skill 4 drops the level term. These are the original game's own files, three skills out of four, before we touched anything.

Seven years of copies by hand​

We started the code base in 2016 and left skills alone until February 2019, when the first version of the composable skill system began: a skill became a tree of nodes, stored as JSON in a column of the database table. The format of the client files changed two weeks after that start, from text to JSON, and the number of copies stayed at three.

After that, every skill change was edited into each copy by hand. Counting the commits that touched a client copy between February 2019 and March 2026 gives 121. By year: 16 in 2019, 27 in 2020, 35 in 2021, 2 in 2022, 12 in 2023, 8 in 2024, 15 in 2025 and 6 in 2026 up to March.

The server copy was the worst of the three: before the YAML files, skill data was edited in the database table with no versioning. Git holds two SQL snapshots of skill_proto, from 2019, and nothing after. A balance change on the server left no diff, no review and no line a client edit could be checked against.

The cost showed whenever a change was big. In April 2021 the new damage calculation left a note in its own commit message: the work still to do was skill_proto, locale, client pack, apply client side. Four places for one idea.

Twice we tried to close the gap by hand. In November 2022 a commit, "skill desc reflects the server", rewrote the tooltip formulas. Skills 1 and 2 had been showing something different from the server until that day:

-           "poly": "0.5*TotalPhysicalAtk+((TotalPhysicalAtk/3)*k)*0.82"
+           "poly": "830*k+(TotalPhysicalAtk-AuraPhysicalAtk)*1.2"

How long that tooltip had been wrong is not knowable, because the server side was not in git. In September 2024 we moved the skill indices into the shared core so client and server could not disagree about a skill's number. That was the first real step to one copy, and it covered the vnums only.

March 2026: the server copy enters git​

On 6 March 2026 the skill proto started loading from configuration files instead of the database: 211 YAML files, one per skill, about 6,100 lines. A tool read the live database over a tunnel and wrote them out. For the first time the server copy was content in a repository, and since 5 March 70 commits have touched the skill configs, all of them reviewable.

It did not reduce the copies. The client still read its own two files, so there were still three, and now two of them could at least be diffed.

One burn, two numbers​

Skill 93 is the dragon's roar. It sets the target on fire, and the chance to do so is a per-mille value, so the server config said successPctPoly: 50*k: 5% at full skill. The client tooltip said 50%.

The tooltip had been changed in September 2025:

      - key: $firepct
-      poly: max(100,IQ*2*k)
+      poly: (500*k)/10

The versioned config said 5% from its first day, 6 March 2026, and the tooltip said 50% until we fixed it on 29 July. That is under five months of disagreement that git can show. Nothing shows what the database held before March, so the disagreement is not dated earlier.

Deleting a copy to see what it hid​

By July 2026 the plan was the obvious one: stop keeping three copies. The client would read the server's skill files, and the tooltip would take its numbers from them. A tooltip that quotes a number is a client-side view of a server value, so there is nothing to keep in sync.

The reason was the limit: three hand-kept copies meant every skill had three places to be wrong. The tooltips were the first client of one copy, not the motive for it.

Read it as two systems in one picture: the top three lines are what we had, three sources feeding three readers, and the bottom is what a skill is now, one file feeding the same three.

The work went in steps, each one found by trying it:

  • 28 July: the engine's point names moved into the shared core, so the two sides read one table instead of two maps that had drifted. 167 files.
  • 29 July: the tooltip stopped carrying its own polys. The commit message reads: the description file carried 281 polys copied from the skill configs, and seventeen had drifted. The client stopped reading its own table and read the server's configs. A reference that does not land is a boot error.
  • 30 July: the cast range, declared once. targetRange and client.castRange were two authored numbers for one concept, and they disagreed on 7 of the 129 skills that declared both.
  • 4 August: one flag vocabulary. The client flag block went away and both parsers read one list. It had been telling the two sides different things on 25 skills for the buffable-NPC flag alone.
  • 5 August: the tooltips became one file per skill, and the client reads a policy.
  • 6 August: the client skill table, 1,351 lines, was deleted.

None of this was found by reading. It was found by trying to have one copy: the audit lines above, and the rest, only showed once a copy that could have hidden them was gone. Deleting one of two copies is a check that review never gave us.

What broke on the way​

On 30 July we restored five client flag lists that had been lost to a folded YAML scalar. Four skills went inert. Without the flag that says a skill needs a target, the client sends a target id of 0 and the server refuses the cast because there is no victim. That is the cost of the move: moving a copy means the flag you forgot to move turns into a skill that does nothing.

The audit had other lines. Skill 19 declared the weapons it needs without the flag that made the client enforce them, so the only enforcer, the client, did not. The client added the bow-range point to every skill's reach while the server added it to none, so a melee skill grew because the player wore a bow-range item.

One file, and what it costs​

Skill 1 is now one server-owned file: flags: once, range: 450 once, a client: block with presentation only (job, icon, motion index, grade count), and a description section that names the formula by reference. The tooltip is words and two variables, $val and $targets, with no formula in it. The client loads the server's skill folder, and the folder is staged into the client pak as one entry.

If a description names a reference that does not resolve, the server refuses it at boot, so a typo fails at startup instead of on whichever player first opens that tooltip.

The tooltip file went from 2,096 lines to 113 per-skill files of 873 lines in all, with no formula copies in them. The cost is real: the skill engine itself grew, from about 5,400 lines to 9,528, because the checks that keep one copy honest are code. The gain is in copies, not lines.

entry.title: A script that waits on the server
entry.summary: A quest coroutine could wait for a player and for nothing else. The bridge made any script wait on the database or another core with a receipt, an owner and a pin, and three lifetime bugs showed what that costs.
entry.content:
A quest script can wait for exactly one thing: a player answering a question the C++ asked on its behalf. q.select stops the coroutine, the manager sends the choices to the client, and the next packet from that client resumes the script on the following line. There is no way to write "ask the database and continue when it answers", and no way to write "ask the other core where this dungeon lives".

The commit that added it, on 2024-10-09, touched 34 files and added 1,538 lines. The bridge source alone changed by about 500 lines, and a new 299-line header tracks who owns which coroutine. A bug in that header was still being found on 2026-04-08. In between sit a coroutine that restarted from the top, references the garbage collector could take from under the C++, a yield that did not belong in C++, and a disconnect that resumed scripts on a character that was already gone. This post is that mechanism and the three bugs that shaped it.

Why quests were not enough told why the short-lived quest coroutine was the biggest flaw, and How the quest manager works, and what Forge changed showed the one global state it runs in. Neither showed what replaced the yield. The quest manager still exists and still runs in parallel with Luna; this is about the coroutine Luna runs next to it.

A yield the C++ must foresee​

The quest yield is a closed set. The C++ knows when a script is about to yield, because the yielding functions are the ones that send a dialogue: select, wait, input, confirm. The manager stores the suspended coroutine on the player's quest state, and the client's answer is routed to that player. A new kind of answer needs a new packet, a new switch case and a new yielding function, written in C++.

The limit is not a speed. It is a shape: a script cannot wait for anything the engine did not foresee. A subsystem that needed a database answer therefore did the same thing in C++: send a packet with a header, register a handler for the answer header, and carry the state between the two halves by hand in a table.

Three ways to wait​

The realistic ways to give a script a wait are three.

A per-request callback: the script passes a function, the engine calls it when the answer comes. It works for one wait. It stops working when a feature needs three waits in a row, because the code now nests three functions deep, an error in the second has no way back to the first, and the local variables of the first have to be captured by hand.

An explicit state machine: the feature stores a state in a table, and a handler per answer header advances it. This is what the C++ handlers already were. Every feature carries its own table, its own cleanup and its own "what if the player left" branch.

Yielding calls: the script is written straight-line, and the wait is a call that does not return until the answer arrives. A quest conversation already reads this way. The first bridge commit says so in its own message: yielding versions of the database and main-core sends exist "to allow the script to wait the answer instead of having to setup another handler".

I took the third because the control flow stays in one function, but it moves the problem. A callback is owned by whoever registered it, and the engine forgets it after the call. A suspended coroutine is a piece of script state that the engine holds for an unknown time. Something has to say who can wake it, who can kill it and when it dies if nobody answers.

A receipt, an owner and a deadline​

The bridge keeps a table of coroutine records keyed by an id. A script creates a coroutine with bridge.coro.create_with_player_owner, which runs it immediately up to its first yield. If it ends before yielding, no record survives. If it yields, the record stays.

Three things decide how it wakes.

A receipt token. A wait asks the bridge for a token that packs the coroutine id, an owner type and an owner id, and sends the token inside the request. The other side answers with the token echoed back. The bridge looks the token up and compares the owner it was issued to with the owner on the answer. A wrong owner finds nothing.

An owner. A coroutine can belong to a player or a peer, and one owner can hold many coroutines. When the owner goes away, the bridge closes every coroutine it holds, resuming each one with nil, false.

A deadline. A wait can carry a timeout. The bridge keeps the deadlines in a priority queue and cancels lazily: a deadline that has already been answered is marked dead and skipped when it surfaces.

The script side is two helpers. This is the code today, from the helper that waits on the database:

helper.sys.game.yield_db = function(header, message, desc_handler, ...)
    local coro_id = bridge.coro.get_current_id()
    if not coro_id then 
        error("yield_db outside a coroutine")
    end
    -- db is the peer 0
    local receipt = bridge.coro.generate_receipt_token(coro_id, bridge.coro.COROUTINE_OWNER.PEER, 0)
    forge.sys.game.send_db(header, message, desc_handler, receipt)
    return coroutine.yield(...)
end

The token is made, the packet goes out with it, and the coroutine yields. The game loop is single-threaded, so the answer cannot overtake the yield: it is processed later, on the same loop, after the script is suspended. The database side answers with the same token.

One feature end to end shows the shape. The vote buff window sends a redeem message from the client. The handler validates it, then starts a coroutine owned by that player and returns at once. The coroutine claims the vote in the database with a 2 second timeout:

local res, ok = forge_helper.coro.with_timeout(2000,
    forge_helper.sys.game.yield_db, "claim", req:SerializeToString())
if not ok then
    send_result(ch, false, 0, nil)
    return
end

local parsed = pb_loader.parse_string(messages.DGVote4BuffClaim, res)
if not parsed.claimed then
    send_result(ch, false, 0, nil)
    return
end

The same function then grants the buff and reports to the client. The database half is a handler that runs SQL and answers with the receipt it was given. There is no registered answer handler on the game side, no table of pending requests and no cleanup branch for a player who left: the owner takes care of that, and ok is false on both a timeout and a close.

Read it from the top. The two exits at the bottom are the reason the bridge exists. A wait can end three ways, and the script sees only two shapes of result.

Two details keep the picture honest. The token is erased before the script resumes, so a duplicate answer finds nothing and is dropped. And after a failed wait the record is removed even if the script yields again, so a script cannot keep waiting after its owner is gone.

The coroutine that restarted from the top​

The first version kept the thread and the coroutine handle in the record and nothing else. They were references only C++ held, and the Lua garbage collector does not see a C++ map. A coroutine suspended for a few seconds on a database answer could be collected while the answer was on its way.

On 2025-01-20 I tried the obvious pin: put the coroutine and its thread on the global state and use the pinned references in their place. It broke differently. A pinned reference is rebuilt on the global state, so the coroutine handle forgot the thread it came from, and the next resume ran the entry function from its first line instead of continuing. I left a note in the source saying exactly that and fixed it two days later, on 2025-01-22, in a change of 8 added lines.

The root cause was not the pin. There were two lifetimes, the C++ record and the Lua garbage collector, and nothing owned the link between them. A pin is how you make the collector respect the record, and the real question is what to pin. The fix pinned the thread and the coroutine, and the pins lived inside the record, so they died with it. After the later cleanup the shape is this: the thread and the entry function are pinned, and the coroutine handle is kept as it is. The code says why:

// store the coroutine as it is because if we pin it to global state the coroutine gets basically reconstructed in the
// global state losing new_thread's state and therefore we won't be able to get the coro id using the corourine.
// This should be safe since we keep the reference in the coda and we are sure the underlying state (new_thread's) won't be collected (it is pinned)

The pins are released in one place, where a coroutine dies, whichever way it dies: answered, timed out, closed by its owner or failed. That is the part I would copy into another engine. The pin and the record are one object with one exit.

Everything C++ holds across a call​

The same bug had a wider form, and I found it from a different side. On 2025-01-01 a commit pinned every long-lived Lua reference that C++ stores: processors, callbacks, guarded calls. A boot-time quest registered the lobby processors from the state the quest manager opens for its scripts. That state is ephemeral, and a reference built on it is eventually collected. When it was, the lobby stopped: no error and no log line, just a lobby that stayed stuck, and every system that went through it stuck with it. "Eventually" is the whole difficulty: the failure depends on when the collector runs, not on what the script did, so no test written around the script reproduces it.

Three months later I centralised it. All references and pins live in the bridge, the game asks for them by id, and the bridge cleans up before the global state is killed. An earlier mistake of the same family was a destructor hook on the forge that operated on a Lua state that was already closed and crashed; on 2024-11-20 I commented and documented it. The rule these share is simple: a reference C++ keeps is C++'s to release, and the release has to happen before the state it points into is gone.

Yielding from C++​

The first yielding sends were C++ functions that sent the packet and called lua_yield themselves. I replaced them on 2025-01-20, the same day as the failed pin. The symptom was a coroutine that started at once, yielded, and could not be resumed by the engine; it finished in a dead state instead of waiting for its answer. The new shape is what is above: token, send and coroutine.yield are three lines of Lua in one visible place, and a script author can read where the script stops. The bridge no longer has a yield function at all.

The lesson I take from it is not about Lua. A suspension point should be visible to the code that suspends. When the function that sends also suspends, the call looks like a send and behaves like a goto.

A disconnect that resumed into a missing character​

A player-owned wait ends when the player leaves, and ending it means running the script. The close resumes each coroutine with nil, false, and the script runs its failure branch: it logs, it may look up the character, it may roll back. That runs inside the disconnect path.

The first order was to erase the player's quest state and then close their coroutines. A failure branch that looked the player up through the quest manager could find nothing. On 2025-05-17 I swapped the two, so the close happens while the character and its state are still there. A continuation never touches a freed character; the character is erased after.

The second bug was in the owner table itself. The table is a multimap, because one owner may hold several coroutines, and the close looked up the owner's key with a single find. It closed the first coroutine and left the rest. The header was written on 2024-10-09 and fixed on 2026-04-08: for about eighteen months, a player who left with two waits open had the first one closed. The second stayed suspended with its ownership erased, until its answer or its timeout came. Nobody noticed it in those eighteen months, which is the point: a leaked wait has no symptom until its answer arrives for an owner who is gone. The fix is the range lookup the container needed from the start.

Both are the same class, and it is the one the design invites: a missed cleanup is a leak that keeps a script alive, and a late cleanup is a script that wakes in a world that moved on.

What it costs​

Every wait is a heap record, two pins, entries in the owner table and the token table, and a timeout object when it has a deadline. That is small next to a request to a database, and it is paid on every wait.

The costs that matter are the invariants for the next author.

  • Every wait needs an owner or a timeout. Without either, a suspended coroutine stays in the table until the process ends.
  • Code after a wait has two result shapes. A script that reads the answer without checking the flag treats a closed owner as an answer.
  • A failed wait removes the record, so a script cannot wait again after one. It has to return.
  • Closing runs script code during a disconnect, so the order of cleanup in the engine is now part of the script contract. The disconnect fix above exists because of it.
  • Erasing the tokens of a coroutine scans the table of live tokens. It is linear in outstanding waits on every resume and death. It has not mattered at the scale of one server, and a server with far more outstanding waits would index tokens by coroutine.

The old quest coroutine had none of these because it could not wait for anything the C++ had not foreseen.

What it made possible​

A script can ask any other part of the system and continue when it answers. Rejoin asks another core where a dungeon lives and warps to the answer: the wait resumes on the first reply from the peers. The vote window asks the database and gives the player a buff. Login hands authentication to a background worker and yields until the result comes back, so the game loop does not wait for it. A script can also open a wait that collects replies from several owners for a fixed time and resumes once with all of them.

None of these needed a new packet type in the engine, a switch case or a registered answer handler on the game side. A feature is a protobuf message, a forge and a handler on the other end.

What a reader can reuse is short:

  • Hand out a receipt that names who may wake the wait, and erase it on the first use.
  • Give every suspension an owner and a deadline, and make failure a different shape of result, not a different call.
  • Pin in the same place you keep the record, and release in the one place the record dies.
  • Make the yield a line of script, not a side effect of a send.

entry.title: 5,000 stones: from 245 ms to 45 ms a frame
entry.summary: How I reduced the work in an RHI crowd frame, and learned which benchmark results not to trust.
entry.content:
A frame with 5,000 stones took 245.0 ms in one RHI build and 45.0 ms in another. The client submitted 1,346,110 draw items before the changes and 10,238 after them. Draw calls fell from 402 to 130.

That comparison came from one machine, alternating two RHI binaries during the same run. It does not compare D3D9 with DirectX 11. The second optimized half of the run was discarded after the machine slowed down, so the result has a limit: it is useful evidence from one run, not a portable promise about another machine.

The scene was grid 5000: a grid of 5,000 characters spawned inside the client, using a stone model, with no server in the measurement. The spacing kept all 5,000 instances in view. That mattered because an empty or culled crowd can make a renderer look very fast.

I left batching for later​

The Metin2 mainline engine used Direct3D 8. In that engine, skinning ran on the CPU, and each particle had its own draw call. The D3D9 pipeline remained untouched until 2024. I migrated the renderer to an RHI over DirectX 11 at the end of 2025 and the start of 2026, in 279 migration commits.

Performance, quality, and extensibility increased through that work. I do not have a D3D9 versus DirectX 11 benchmark to put a number on the performance change.

The 2025 plan documents changed during development: timing, effort, approaches, and solutions all drifted. In January 2026, I moved the model renderer back to a per-instance draw call and left optimization and batching for later. The change touched 38 files. In August, more than seven months after that decision, I returned to the cost of submitting and drawing a crowd.

The full comparison was much larger than one change. Each optimization below was measured against its own neighboring build or setting, so the individual gains overlap and do not add up to the difference between 245.0 and 45.0 ms.

The same stone had 89 rigid meshes​

The stone model in the grid had 89 rigid meshes. Before consolidation, the renderer enumerated those meshes separately for each instance and each relevant pass. Instancing reduced the number of API draws, but the CPU still had to collect and process the draw items.

I merged compatible single-material rigid meshes when the model loaded. The merged geometry used the skinned vertex format, with one full-weight bone per vertex. Each member kept its own transform through the bone palette, so meshes did not need to share a bone to share a draw.

The grouping still had limits. Material, material type, and tangent validity had to agree. The merge accepted single-UV models and up to 256 members per draw; it did not turn every rigid mesh into one universal batch.

The path for the stone changed like this:

In the per-change grid 5000 comparison, the frame went from 118.2 to 66.9 ms. Draw items fell from 897,454 to 10,238, and draws from 306 to 130. Those figures describe that change against its own predecessor, not the complete optimization wave.

The draw count alone had hidden much of the work. A frame can issue relatively few draws and still spend a great deal of time preparing them.

I stopped uploading unchanged poses​

The renderer also rebuilt and uploaded bone palettes for skeletons whose poses had not advanced. A standing crowd could send matrices that were already in GPU memory.

I gave each skeleton a resident palette at a fixed offset. A compute scatter rewrote it when the pose advanced. On grid 5000, the reported comparison went from 122.5 to 119.3 ms; 2.0 ms of that difference was attributed to skipping unchanged poses.

The palette had to live as long as its skeleton. Keeping data resident only helps if its owner and the condition for updating it are clear.

Particle state stayed on the GPU​

I moved particle simulation into a resident VRAM buffer updated by compute. The CPU retained birth, death, and texture-frame bookkeeping. Terrain-conformed particles retained CPU simulation.

The compute path had to preserve the behavior of the existing effects. For example, air resistance remained frame-rate dependent, and the order of rotation, scale, color, gravity, resistance, and position updates mattered to effects authored against those formulas.

On omo 1000, a scene with 1,000 stones and ground effects, the reported comparison went from 32.3 to 27.6 ms. That was another comparison between RHI builds.

I also consolidated overlay material effects. Instead of giving each enabled overlay its own geometry redraw, I expressed its per-pixel contribution and evaluated the enabled contributions in one additive redraw. Effects that needed their own vertex shader or rasterizer state kept a separate pass.

The sweep caught an empty world​

I added an unattended sweep that logged the client in, built a scene, held a fixed camera, measured a 240-frame window with vsync and frame pacing off, and wrote a CSV row before moving to the next instance count.

The client-side grid removed the server from that measurement. Server spawn commands put many mobs close to the player and left the server simulating them; at high counts, the server could fall over and leave the client with little to draw. The sweep recorded how many instances were actually spawned and drawn.

That count saved some wrong results. Three sweeps reported 4.1 ms frames for 5,000 instances. They had measured an empty world.

I alternated configurations within a run because the laptop's clock changed enough to overwhelm the gains being measured. The same binary recorded 35.95 ms in the morning and 69.07 ms in the afternoon with identical draw-item counts. Both numbers could be true for that machine, but comparing them would say more about its clock than the renderer.

The full 245.0 to 45.0 ms comparison alternated binaries, each with its own root pack. Shaders lived in the pack, so a binary needed the pack that matched it. During the second optimized half, the machine dropped to roughly a third of its speed while the draw-item count remained 10,238. I discarded that half.

A correct picture needed its own test​

A faster frame is not useful if an effect disappeared. I compared captures with a change off, off again, and then on, using the first pair to establish how much the scene changed on its own.

One visual gate still missed a regression. A terrain-conformed additive decal was drawn after effect meshes, so alpha-blended groups above it no longer attenuated it. The six-decal test scene had no such group above the decal. It could show whether the grid's geometry matched the ground, but it could not show the compositing error. The login screen's waterfall could.

A visual test has to contain the interaction a change can break. A scene that exercises the changed geometry may still be unable to expose a draw-order mistake.

entry.title: Extended, never wrapped
entry.summary: How materials extended particle effects without replacing the paths that already referenced them.
entry.content:
In the Metin2 mainline engine, a particle draws one texture at a time and has one color operation. Its color curves give it one color across the whole particle. I wanted to deliver visually appealing surface effects without hooking into the engine every time, and to make effects more expressive and higher quality.

The old vocabulary could tint a particle over its lifetime, but it could not give that particle a white hot core and a violet edge, burn it away through noise, or scroll layers across it. Actor surface looks had their own limit: gear quality colors came from hardcoded render configuration tables. A new look beyond those choices meant engine work.

Rage was the first client of the extension. The limit was the reason for it.

Two days of YAML​

On September 30, I started with surface materials as YAML profiles. An effect group named a material profile, and per actor layers resolved into an instance slot so the looks would not split batches.

By October 2, the YAML catalog was gone. It had lived for two days.

The catalog introduced a second language alongside the text language the engine already used for its visual formats. It also needed three registry files with hand assigned IDs, a name lookup that resolved against different registries depending on the element, and profiles that could not be parameterized where they were used. Model masks lived in a separate binding that the person editing the model could not see. The world editor dropped the new keys when it saved an effect.

The existing formats already had a simpler pattern: keep the settings in local text files and reference other resources by path. I brought materials into that language, along with parameterized materials, model masks, and attachment bundles. The loader also gained whole line comments and parameters.

The rule became: MSE is extended, never wrapped. Existing references still name an .mse. An effect can name a material by path, and the client puts each distinct material into its GPU tables when it is first referenced.

The diagram shows where the references go:

The effect owns behavior: when particles spawn, how long they live, how they move, and their texture, blend, and color curves. The material owns how their pixels are shaded. A model mask identifies regions of a model, and a bundle says what attaches to an actor together.

The lesson I took from the two days is that every site that already names an effect should keep naming it. A parallel registry gives each of those sites a second route to maintain.

A group without a material remains the old effect. Older clients ignore the new material keys, and they skip new group types while drawing the rest of the file. Keeping the existing reference as the entry point let the extension travel through paths that already worked.

How effect paths get registered is outside this post.

One gradient on one particle​

Before the extension, giving a particle a new color meant changing the color supplied by its curves. Every pixel of that particle received the same color. A texture could contain brightness differences, but the effect could not use those differences to put separate colors across the particle.

Afterward, I could give the particle a material that reads the texture brightness through a gradient. This material also gives the particle emission and glow:

Group Effect
{
    Family               emissive_particle
    Emission             1.6
    Gradient             "d:/ymir work/special/cosmetics/ramps/rage.dds"
    GradientMode         replace
    GradientInput        brightness
    GradientGain         1.2
    GradientLifeShift    0.2
    Group Glow
    {
        Intensity         2.4
        Radius            1
        Color             1 0.667 0.267
        Core              2
        Streaks           6
    }
}

The particle group names that material with one line:

MaterialFile             "d:/ymir work/special/cosmetics/material/effect/rage_flash.msfvx"

The existing effect still controls the particle's motion and lifetime. The material changes its pixels. There is no engine change or engine build for this gradient.

The input texture matters. A brightness gradient on a pure white texture produces one flat color, because every pixel supplies the same value. Using alpha as the input can flood a sprite when its alpha covers the whole quad. The particle gradient tutorial builds the example step by step; the effects and materials reference covers the format.

A day of families, and two things removed​

October 1 brought ribbons on bones, afterimages, distortion, layered materials, a mesh kit, and an impact group with hitstop, impact frames, and radial blur. The layered material could scroll up to three layers, distort them with flow, and use ramps, masks, cutoff, and dissolve.

I also set a rule for accepting a family: it had to do something plain MSE and MDE could not, demonstrated by comparing it with the old effect.

Two additions did not survive the day. Selective glow used a half resolution blur; emissive bloom replaced it that same day. The replacement uses authored emission, builds a six level mip chain, and composites before the UI. It can produce a wide glow in LDR without depending on scene bloom.

A ground decal group and its registry arrived that morning and were retired the same day. Ground particles already did that job. A new effect family needs to earn its place against what the old format can actually do.

The material made the old rage worse​

I applied the rage gradient to the old smoke and ground ring. The smoke lost its mass. The vivid violet ring turned muddy dark crimson because most of the rage gradient is dark.

The improvement came from adding groups designed for materials: implosion embers, a core flash, and nova sparks alongside old groups left untouched. Before assigning a material to an existing group, compare it with the old look. If it is not clearly better, leave the group alone.

I also judge the effect in LDR first. HDR and bloom are off by default and off on many players' machines, so brightness above 1 only appears for players who have them enabled. HDR can add to the look, but the effect needs to read without it.

What the crowd cost​

The materials stood on earlier RHI work and the renderer work described in 5,000 stones. On August 20, particle simulation moved to a GPU resident buffer updated by compute. Overlay effects also stopped drawing the geometry again for each overlay; their contributions went into one additive redraw.

On my bench, I measured a grid of player models on a guild map, using medians over 300 frames:

CrowdBaseRage body surface on every actorFour ribbons and an ember emitter per idle actor
40 actors0.91 ms+0.09 ms+0.13 ms
200 actors1.23 ms+0.12 ms+0.33 ms

Turning glow and distortion on or off stayed within noise. Each added term was below the roughly 1 ms noise floor, so these measurements do not establish a precise cost for the individual features.

Rage became a bundle​

On October 13, rage moved from its own polymorph state to broadcast affect 605, a forge file, and an attachment bundle. The bundle brings the actor effects and surfaces together. An exit group plays a vanish when the affect really ends. The rage post covers that move.

Bundles are now referenced by the sanctuary aura and rage broadcast affects, by gear quality, and by map objects. Item rows support them, although the item effect file has no bundle row yet. Everything else in the game still plays plain effects.

The layered and mesh families shipped as building blocks. Procedural sprites and noise did not reach the quality I wanted, and their generated example art remains below that bar. The examples wait for an artist.

entry.title: 22 weeks planned, a triangle on day 5
entry.summary: Replacing a Direct3D 9 renderer in stages, from the first device wrapper to retiring the old device.
entry.content:
I threw away a D3D9 shader layer about 20 months after the port that introduced it. Cascaded shadows had landed on December 21, 2025. Two days later, I started the RHI migration.

The Metin2 mainline engine used Direct3D 8. Its state manager cached render states and avoided a device call when the requested value matched the cache. Rendering code could also call the device directly. Those two paths had to agree: a direct state change bypassed the cache, so a later request through the manager could be skipped even though the device held a different value.

In April 2024, I ported the pipeline to D3D9. The old pipeline had been untouched until then. The port brought the first shaders and GPU skinning: the model renderer supplied bone matrices to a vertex shader, which weighted the transformed position and normal by the vertex's bone indices and weights.

By December 2025, models were already using shaders. UI and effects still used fixed-function rendering. The Metin2 mainline engine had baked terrain shadows and a projected character shadow; the D3D9 renderer gained cascaded shadows on December 21. That shader layer had a short life.

The plan and the triangle​

The 2025 plan estimated 22 to 24 weeks. I changed the plan repeatedly while developing: timing, effort, approaches, and solutions all drifted. The dates here follow the work that landed, rather than treating the plan as a record of what happened.

My first migration commit was on December 23, 2025. It introduced the RHI and wrapped the existing device. I also put an ImGui panel in on day one. The wrapper gave me a way to introduce an interface while the old renderer still existed; the panel gave the work a place to expose its state from the start.

On December 26, I initialized DX11. On December 27, the fifth calendar day counting December 23 as day one, a triangle rendered through DX11. A triangle proved that the new path could issue a draw. It did not mean the game had migrated.

I wrote a DX9 backend too. On December 27, the same day as the triangle, I rolled back the forwarding of the old device's commands into the RHI, and on January 13 I deleted the whole DX9 backend, close to 3,000 lines. The idea of keeping toggles between backends was abandoned. Supporting two paths during a migration has a cost even when the end goal is one renderer.

Bridges kept the game moving​

I used bridges while pieces of the renderer crossed the boundary. A DX11-to-DX9 bridge appeared on December 29. On December 31, I added the render graph and wrapped the old render loop in it. On January 13, the RHI took ownership of the swapchain while D3D9 ran headless.

Model migration started twice: on December 31, I removed an earlier attempt and added new scaffolding. In January, I deliberately returned the model renderer to a draw per instance, with batching to follow. Getting a path across the boundary and optimizing it were separate jobs.

The transition had an endpoint. I removed the DX11-to-DX9 bridge on February 25 and the DX9-to-RHI bridge the next day. On February 28, day 68, I retired the old D3D9 device. Temporary compatibility code needs a way out, or it becomes another permanent rendering path.

A frame through the RHI​

The idea that held was to put resource creation and drawing behind an interface, then move rendering work through it a piece at a time.

The old model path sent bone matrices to a D3D9 shader. In the RHI renderer, the application prepares a frame, builds a render graph, and executes its passes through a command buffer. The model renderer submits work through that interface, and the DX11 backend issues the API draws. The default forward frame uses the graph too.

The graph compiler orders passes from their resource dependencies, removes passes whose outputs are unreferenced, and calculates resource lifetimes. The forward scene pass still contains an ordered sequence of scene work, including the map, actors, water, and effects. Moving to a graph did not make every part of the frame independent.

On March 21, I merged the branch. It contained 279 commits; the client changes covered 574 files, with 81,779 lines added and 74,532 removed. Performance, quality, and extensibility increased greatly through the work. I do not have a D3D9-versus-DX11 measurement to put a number on that comparison.

The renderer continued to change after the merge. In one later benchmark, grid 5000 went from 245.0 ms to 45.0 ms, while draw items fell from 1,346,110 to 10,238. Those figures compare two RHI builds, not D3D9 against DX11.

entry.title: A point used to be a branch in the damage code
entry.summary: In the Metin2 mainline engine a bonus point does nothing until some function reads it, and a conditional bonus is one more branch in the damage code. How a scoped point bump turned that into a hook, a skills-only detour that traits superseded, and what still lives in the damage code.
entry.content:
In the Metin2 mainline engine a bonus point is a number on a character, and it does nothing. The effect exists only because some function reads that number and does something with it. If the bonus has a condition, the condition is an if in that function, and the function is usually the damage code. When I started on this engine, every new conditional bonus meant another branch there.

This post follows that limit through four stages: the Metin2 mainline branch, the redesign that kept it, the point bump that removed the need for it, and a skills-only detour that traits superseded.

Two lines in the damage function​

This is stock code, from the Metin2 mainline damage function:

if (IsAffectFlag(AFF_TERROR))
    dam = (int32_t) (dam * (95 - GetSkillPower(SKILL_TERROR) / 5) / 100);

if (IsAffectFlag(AFF_HOSIN))
    dam = dam * (100 - GetPoint(POINT_RESIST_NORMAL_DAMAGE)) / 100;

The point POINT_RESIST_NORMAL_DAMAGE is a stat. The buff AFF_HOSIN is a flag. The only thing that joins them is these two lines, and the join lives inside the function that resolves a hit. Block, dodge, reflect, HP steal and the mana shield are written the same way in the same file: a point, and a hand-written reader.

The Metin2 mainline engine has fewer than 150 of these points. We started the code base in 2016 with 192 slots. Today there are 324. Each one that is more than a plain stat needs its own reader somewhere in the server, and in the client when the player has to see the number.

What a new bonus touched​

A bonus is not only the branch. The point has to exist on the server and on the client, travel in a packet, show on a Python page, and be written into the item prototype tables. Counting the commits that added one:

  • lifesteal percent, June 2020: 9 files;
  • defence penetration, November 2019: 16 files, across server, client C++, Python and the proto tools;
  • def_penetration_pvp with a reflect rewrite, March 2024: 15 files;
  • skill damage against monsters, spec skill damage and a slow adder, June 2020: 23 files.

Two of those are mixed commits that carry other work, so "touched" is the honest word, not "needed". The range of 9 to 23 files is real all the same, and none of those commits gave a bonus a condition. They only added a number that a reader still had to find.

The 2021 redesign kept the branch​

In April 2021 we redesigned the damage calculation, in two commits on the 9th and the 13th. The first touched 28 files and the second 24, with penetration and pierce rewritten from the ground up. The four large server files alone carried over 2,000 changed lines.

The hosin branch went through it unchanged. The same two lines were in the same function after the redesign, and they were still there five years later. They left in July 2026.

The redesign changed how damage is computed. It did not change who gets to say what a point means. That stayed with whoever wrote the next if. Another 2021 commit that year added a conditional rule as a constant in the hit code (the part of a critical chance above 75% counted at half), and a table added in October 2021 to map skills to adder bonuses had a key that was a point instead of a skill, so it could never match. It sat there silently until it was retired in July 2026.

Four copies of the damage pipeline​

The branches had one more consequence. The defence half of the pipeline existed four times: in the melee hit, in two arms of the ranged shot, and in the skill damage function. Each copy had drifted. The skill path read one set of defence values and the autos read another; the PC bow arm applied the attack multiplier twice, squaring it into the shot. In July 2026 the four became one resolver, and the two real bugs (the doubled multiplier, and the magic shot that used a narrower integer) were fixed instead of carried over. That is getting ahead of the story, and it matters for one reason: while the branches lived inside four copies, nothing could move out of them.

The bump point​

The idea that held is small. A trait is a piece of behavior gated by an affect. While the affect is up, the trait gets hooks around a hit: before damage is dealt, before damage is taken, and so on. In a hook it can say "for this hit, this character has +15 of this point". The damage formula reads the point as it always did. When the hit ends, the bump is gone.

Nothing in the formula learns about the condition. It is in the hook, in Lua or in C++, next to the affect that owns it. The engine side is a few lines. GetPoint folds in the live bumps:

// Fold in any live trait bump (transient; empty outside a damage frame).
if (!m_pointBump.empty()) {
    auto bit = m_pointBump.find(static_cast<uint16_t>(type));
    if (bit != m_pointBump.end()) val += bit->second;
}

The traits framework landed on 11 June 2026, 17 files, with about 3,100 lines added and 15 removed. Its first client was the mayhem augments, the conditional bonuses an arena mode wanted: more damage while your HP is low, stacks per kill, a bonus that depends on the target. Those are the cases where a point plus a number collapses, and they were what we had at hand. They were the first client. The limit was the one in the previous sections.

Before, an augment was a row in a pool: an apply, and a base value.

local POOL = {
    -- Damage (8)
    { apply = apply.PHYS_ATT_BONUS,           base = 60   },
    { apply = apply.MAGIC_ATT_BONUS,          base = 60   },

After, the same kind of augment is a definition with a gate and a hook. This one is the code today:

traits.define{
    id   = "cold_blood",
    gate = { affect = affect.name_map.AUGMENT_COLD_BLOOD },
    hooks = {
        ---@param ch LPCHARACTER
        ---@param victim LPCHARACTER
        ---@param ctx forge.sys.game.traits.CTX
        on_damage_dealt_pre = function(ch, victim, dam_type, ctx)
            if ch:get_hp_pct() < 80 then
                ctx.bump_point(point.ATTBONUS_HUMAN, 15)
                dbg(ch, "cold_blood +15 ATTBONUS_HUMAN (hp_pct=" .. ch:get_hp_pct() .. ")")
            end
        end,
    },
}

The first rewrite of the augments onto traits, on 11 June, touched 8 files and none of them was C++. The next day "all-in as traits" touched 7, again with no C++. The battle royale in October touched 72 files with no C++ either. A bonus with a condition stopped costing an engine change.

What broke: nested damage​

Nine days later the bump leaked. Nested damage on the same character (an area hit, a chain, a proc) wiped the pending bumps of the outer hit while the deltas stayed applied, and one augment's minus 20 compounded until the damage was near zero. The first version applied bumps to the points directly and reverted them afterwards, and a recompute of the points in the middle of a bump could not tell what to revert.

The fix on 20 June had three parts: a guard that can nest (mark and restore, not clear), a refusal for a bump with no damage guard open (it is logged and ignored), and an overlay. The bumps live in a transient map folded into GetPoint, which is what the excerpt above shows. A recompute in the middle of a bump can no longer desync it.

A skills-only detour​

On 20 July we added a second interface to the platform, a mechanic that skills could implement, with a lazy host on the character. It dispatched lifecycle, use-gate, cost, damage-dealt and point-cap hooks to named mechanics instead of affect-flag tests, and the first mechanic was a charge skill. On the 21st hosin, the mana shield, terror and stealth moved onto it, off their affect flags.

It was an exploration. Once I realized it was superseded by traits, I steered to them. On the 22nd the gate and the definition were split, a native C++ backend was added to traits, and the same four behaviors moved again, from the mechanic platform to traits. On the 24th the interface was retired: 643 lines in, 501 out, five days. Charge had been its last implementer, and what the platform carried ended up as a trait, a member of the skill class and two predicates.

The resolver, and the erosion that left it​

On 26 July the four copies of the pipeline became one resolver. The differences the copies had earned were kept as explicit policy fields; the two bugs were fixed. The change was 5 files, 433 lines added and 397 removed.

Once there was one resolver, the buff erosion could leave it. Resist against a buff's defence had been an inline if chain in each copy, and the resolver first folded it into one table of three entries: a flag, a monster resist column and a bonus point. The next day that table went too. Defence erosion became a trait that bumps the defence point in a damage-taken hook before the resolver reads it (19 files), and attack buff erosion and the weapon binding followed the same day (27 files). That also retired a double count, where the resist was stripped from the raw bonus and then the eroded defence multiplied again.

This is the point I would take to another engine. The bump needed one place where the formula reads a point. Until the four copies were one, the hook sites would have had to be added four times, and each copy would have grown its own idea of what the hook may do.

The Metin2 mainline branch, today, is a trait. It is native C++, the smallest one there is: it multiplies basic-attack damage by the same resist point as the two stock lines, now attached to whatever affect binds it. Traits are registered from C++ and from Lua, hosin on one side and cold blood on the other.

What it did not change​

Line count is not the gain. The damage file is longer than before traits, because the hook sites live there. The calls that test an affect flag by hand are 20 in the server today, down from 73 in June.

A Lua trait can sit at every position inside the damage formula; only the cap on a computed point is native-only, for call frequency. Block, dodge, reflect, HP and SP steal, and the on-hit and on-kill recovery bonuses are still read by hand in the damage code.

entry.title: Eleven branches, three functions, one list
entry.summary: Who may hit whom lived in eleven branches over three functions, each dropped in wherever it fit. How the attack rules went from the Metin2 mainline engine to one ordered list that events join and leave.
entry.content:
On the day before we cut it, the question "may this player hit that one?" was answered by eleven branches spread over three functions, plus the guild-war helper that all three of them call. Five of the eleven sat in the attack check, four in the damage handler and two in the buff check. Each had been added at whatever line was convenient, and the order between them was an accident of history.

That is a tolerable mess until an event has to live in it. The risk I saw was this: any event, Christmas for example, could break normal gameplay, because the attack code path was free for all. There was one shared predicate, every hit in the game ran through it on every map all year, and an event's rule had to be written into it.

What the Metin2 mainline engine did with an event​

The attack predicate we inherited already showed the habit. It asks what the attacker is riding, and the answer is a switch over mount ids: thirty-eight of them, three of which are event mounts for Ramadan, Halloween and Christmas. Every event that shipped a mount had to put its id into the player-versus-player rule. Whichever way the unlisted mounts fall, an event's attack behaviour hung on a hard-coded list inside a rule that has nothing to do with events.

Killer mode, the flag that marks a player as a murderer, was set from inside the same predicate, in six places. Asking "can A attack B" could flag A as a killer as a side effect.

Christmas reached further than the mount. The monster state machine has a branch for the Christmas tree: on one regular hunting map, if the xmas_tree event flag is set, aggressive monsters do not attack first. An event flag changed the behaviour of every aggressive monster on a map people play on all year, from inside the mob AI. That branch is unchanged from the Metin2 mainline engine and is still there today.

2016: nine branches, and a Christmas rule that never fires​

When the 2016 code base was imported, the attack check had nine content branches: a star-attack affect, guild war, a war map, a guild map, the decorated arena, a Christmas monument, the rage dungeon, an anti-matter manager and a seventh-scorpion rule. This is the Christmas one as it stood then.

if ((ch->GetEmpire() == 1 && victim->IsNoAttackShinsu()) ||
    (ch->GetEmpire() == 2 && victim->IsNoAttackChunjo()) ||
    (ch->GetEmpire() == 3 && victim->IsNoAttackJinno()))
    return false;

if (CMobVnumHelper::IsXmasRateMob(victim->GetRaceNum() && ch->GetEmpire() == victim->GetEmpire()))
    return false;

The intent reads as "you may not hit your own empire's Christmas monument". The closing parenthesis is in the wrong place, so the && is evaluated inside the call and a boolean, zero or one, is passed as a monster id. The id range check is never true and the line never denies anything. It has been evaluated on every melee swing, skill cast and projectile contact since, on every map, for a seasonal event. The real guard for that event lives somewhere else: the event manager drops same-empire kills, and the monuments hook into the damage and death code. One event, four places, three of them in shared combat code.

This is a risk, not an incident. It is what "free for all" looks like: a line that is always false is harmless, and a line that is almost always false is a bet.

2020 to 2025: retiring an event meant cutting branches out of shared code​

Removing systems taught the same lesson from the other side. In April 2020 we removed the decorated arena: 35 files, 2,268 lines deleted. In July of that year the rage dungeon, anti-matter, boss manager and others went, 46 files and 3,812 lines, including the lines they had left in the attack check. On 2025-04-12 the old three-way war, the castle event, the battle arena event and the rest of the old event logic followed: 52 files, 6,920 lines out.

None of those were clean deletions of a feature. Each had to reach into shared code, and the 2025 one went through the attack function, the damage function, the death function, the horse code and the death timer, looking for the pieces the events had left in them. I forgot pieces more than once.

Meanwhile the branches fought each other. In November 2023 the combat refactor needed a series of fixes in a week: the new damage handler checked the victim twice and never the attacker. One of those fixes put "party mates cannot hit each other" at the top of the attack check. Above the arena branch and the guild war branch, that meant party mates could not fight each other in an arena or a guild war. It stayed that way for 29 months, until the cut moved the rule below the arbiters. A branch's position was a rule, and nobody had chosen it.

The cut: one list, first registered, first asked​

On 2026-04-30 we replaced the branches with a registry. An arbiter is a name, a guard that says whether the arbiter owns this pair of characters, and a rule that answers allow, deny or pass. The registry walks its list in registration order. The first arbiter whose guard fires and whose rule does not pass has the answer. This is the walk as it is today.

BattleVerdict CBattleArbiterRegistry::Resolve(LPCHARACTER att, LPCHARACTER vic) const
{
    for (const Arbiter& a : m_arbiters) {
        if (!a.guard(att, vic)) continue;

        BattleVerdict v = a.can_attack(att, vic);
        switch (v) {
            case BattleVerdict::Allow: return BattleVerdict::Allow;
            case BattleVerdict::Deny:  return BattleVerdict::Deny;
            case BattleVerdict::Pass:  continue;   // arbiter declined this call
        }
    }
    return BattleVerdict::Pass;
}

The change was 24 files, with 52 lines touched in the shared attack code. Look at where the registry sits in the diagram: after the absolute vetoes, before the default rules, so an arbiter can never be overruled by the party rule and never needs to know about it.

The arena registered first, from C++, and it was the first client of the registry, not the reason for it. The reason was the shape above: a third mode meant editing the shared function, a Lua event could not state its own rules without a C++ patch, and the position of every guard was implicit. The arena's registration was gone 36 days later, replaced by a team session that does the same job from the other side.

What an event costs now​

Guild war moved to Lua on 2026-06-02, and its referee registers one arbiter per war. Land deployment registers from C++, at boot, since September. Battle royale, on 2026-10-20, registers 17 lines of Lua that deny attacks until the game is playing and pass otherwise.

EvE classic is the clearest case, because it is an event in the Christmas sense: it exists for a while on one map. It registered its combat rule on 2026-05-29, a week after the event itself landed.

local VERDICT = forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry.BATTLE_VERDICT
eve_classic.battle_handle = forge.sys.game.battle_arbiter_registry.register(
    "eve:" .. id,
    function(att, vic) return att:get_map_index() == map_index and vic:get_map_index() == map_index end,
    function(att, vic)
        if not forge.game.ue_eve_manager:is_engaged(id) then return VERDICT.Deny end
        if att:is_pc() and vic:is_pc() and att:get_empire() ~= vic:get_empire() then
            return VERDICT.Allow
        end
        return VERDICT.Deny
    end)

On that map only players of different empires may fight, and only once the fight is engaged, not while people are still gathering. At teardown the event calls unregister with the handle and the rule is gone. Compare that with the Christmas monument line: the rule exists between setup and teardown, only where its guard holds, and outside that it is not in the list at all. The shared attack code did not change for it.

Retiring is the same story reversed. Nothing is left in the attack, damage or death code to hunt for, because the event never wrote anything there. And the sibling breakage has no place to come from: a new arbiter cannot reorder the old ones, and the party rule has one position that everyone can read.

What is still in the engine​

The domain is the honest exception. It still has its own branch in both the attack check and the damage handler, on neither an arbiter nor a session. The Christmas monument line and the Christmas tree branch in the mob AI also remain: the registry did not move them, because they were never in the part it replaced.

Warp permission is still a hard-coded check in the character class. Item use sits on top of a policy of its own, with about twenty hard-coded branches in front of it, and it has its own history of silent breakage: when the lobby was rewritten in November 2024 the arena potion gates were commented out, and they stayed that way for 18 months until the item use policy restored them.

The default PvP rules stay in C++ on purpose. Party, empire and PK mode are the stock rule that the list falls through to. What changed is that the stock rule is now the end of a list that events can join and leave, instead of the place events had to be written into.

entry.title: Rage in 237 lines of Lua, and 1,422 lines of C++ deleted
entry.summary: Every visible effect on a character cost me an engine change, and the effect artist could not work without me. How the bitfield limit led to broadcast affects, and what rage looked like once it moved onto them.
entry.content:
For years, putting a new look on a character meant a change to the engine source, and that change was mine. The effect artist could build the particles, the bones and the surfaces, and then the work stopped until I had edited server C++, client C++ and a Python table, built both sides and shipped them. They could not do their work without me.

The reason was a bitfield. This post is about the limits around it, and about rage, which is the largest feature I moved off it. Rage is the proof that the limits are gone. It is not why they went.

Four bits left, and a field I had already enlarged​

In the Metin2 mainline engine, the only thing a viewer learns about another character's affects is a set of bits. The full affect element goes to its owner. Everyone else gets the AFF_ flags in the character update packet: a bitfield of two 32-bit words. The count of AFF_ values was the first limit, so I enlarged the field from 2 dwords to 3.

That bought room, and the room ran out anyway. At the head of the current tree the highest AFF_ value in use is 91, the field holds 96, and the guard in the flag test rejects everything outside 1 to 95. Four bits remain.

The cost of a bit was never only the bit. Adding AFF_ASHURA in December 2023 touched 5 files: the client instance header, the client player settings header, the shared length header, the server affect header and the server constants table. The client and the server each keep their own copy of the AFF_ list, and they drifted. In November 2023 a commit message says it plainly (translated from Italian): the client AFF effects were realigned with the server ones, by hand.

A seven-entry table for the debuffs the bitfield had no room for​

The target window shows what is on the monster you selected. A bit in the flag word is not enough for that, so in April 2023 I added a fixed table that sent hand-picked effects through the target packet: five entries at first, seven by May. Poison, fire, stun, slow, bleeding, a skill and one buff, each a C++ enum value and a pair in an array.

One of those pairs holds a skill number and an AFF_ number, and the two differ by one, because the server's AFF_ values are shifted by one against the skill numbering. Nobody should have to remember that. The seventh entry, added in May 2023, touched 4 files: the Python target window, the client instance header, the server affect header and the server character code.

The cheater malus in April 2026 is the last visible affect I did the old way. It took 7 files in C++, Python and YAML, one of them the locale text.

One affect type, shown to everyone who can see the character​

The idea that held was to stop describing an effect with a bit and send the affect itself. In June 2026 a server affect can be marked broadcastable, and the full element is relayed to every viewer around the character. The client keeps those elements in a store keyed by the character, and a Python registration says which particle file plays for which affect type.

// Broadcastable affects: relay the full element to everyone who can see the character.
static bool ShouldBroadcastAffect(LPCHARACTER ch, uint32_t dwType)
{
    return AffectManager::instance().IsBroadcastableAffect(dwType);
}

The commit that introduced it says what it routes around: it is now possible to bind a particle without an AFF extension. The affect type is a number the Lua side already owns. No bit, no enum slot, no AFF_ table to keep in step on two sides.

The groundwork was older than the feature. The affect manager that took the save, clear-on-death and no-duration-decrease rules out of C++ macros and into a config file dates from June 2024. In late May and early June 2026 Lua gained the same doors, so a forge can add a name, mark an affect as not saved, or keep it through death. Traits arrived on 11 June, and broadcast the next day.

The first client was the mayhem augment looks, 20 trait affects in the first broadcastable list, plus the buff that used to be the seventh row of the target table. It was a client, not the motive. The motive was in the previous sections. The target table is gone, and nothing replaced its rows with new rows.

In July 2026 the good, bad and party classification of affects also left C++: 54 case lines went out of the character affect code into data. They had drifted from the dispel arrays they were meant to match, and they grew one skill at a time with no owner. That was a separate step, after broadcast, and I do not claim it came before.

Rage, before: a state machine with its own wire​

Rage is a good test because it is old and it touches everything. It is not new; it is in the first commit of the 2016 code base, with its own server module, its own dungeon and its own quest. The server module lived through 17 commits until October 2026.

Its state lived outside the affect system. It kept its own state object per character (points, remaining time, cool-down, an active flag, a sub-rage flag, a refresh event), turned the player into a polymorph per race, and told the client about it with two character state flags of its own. It needed:

  • a server-to-server packet to trigger rage on all cores,
  • three columns in the player table for the gauge, the cool-down and the saved state,
  • a branch inside the affect-adding function that refused rage affects,
  • four quest functions to read and fill the gauge, and a 133-line quest to fill it from an item,
  • GM commands, and hooks in the kill, death and logout paths.

Its art was wired in the client as well. Each look was an enum slot and a row in a C++ table with a file path in it, and the motion files per race were registered in code.

Rage, after: an affect and a forge​

On 13 October 2026 one commit replaced all of that. Rage is now the affect AFFECT_RAGE (605), sub-rage is 617, and rage.forge owns the rest: start and stop (an affect with a duration), the skill grant, the /rage command router, the global trigger over the forge peer-to-peer channel, and a rage_charge trait that fills a charge stored in a quest flag from damage dealt, taken and healed. This is the registration, at the top of the file as it stands today.

affect.add_name_definition("RAGE_CHARGE", 618)
affect.add_broadcastable(affect.name_map.RAGE)
